title: Why do we use partitions (parallelism, scalability, ordering within a partition)?
keyPoints: Partitions enable parallelism: a consumer group can have at most as many active consumers as there are partitions.
Partitions enable horizontal scalability: they can be spread across many brokers so a topic's data and load are not confined to one machine.
Partitions define the ordering boundary: Kafka guarantees strict ordering within a partition, and the key controls which partition a record lands in.
The partition count is effectively permanent because increasing it changes key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering for existing keys.
A poorly chosen key causes skew where one partition gets most of the traffic and becomes a bottleneck while others sit idle.
Too few partitions caps parallelism and throughput; too many partitions increase metadata overhead and leader election time.

s1_definition.oneliner: Partitions let Kafka process many records in parallel and scale across machines, while still keeping strict order for all records that share the same key.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Partition** – an ordered, append-only log within a topic that is the unit of parallelism, ordering, and storage distribution in Kafka.
- **Parallelism** – the ability to process multiple records simultaneously by assigning different partitions to different consumers in a consumer group.
- **Horizontal scalability** – distributing a topic's partitions across many brokers so that both data and processing load scale with the cluster size.
- **Ordering guarantee** – Kafka's promise that records within a single partition are always read in the order they were written, controlled by the choice of message key.
- **Partition key** – a value attached to a record that Kafka hashes to choose the target partition, ensuring records with the same key always land in the same partition.
- **Partition skew** – an imbalance where one partition receives disproportionately more traffic than others due to a poorly chosen key, creating a bottleneck.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has one giant ledger book and only one clerk can write in it at a time: everyone queues up and it is painfully slow. Now imagine the bank splits the ledger into six books (partitions) and assigns one clerk to each book. Six clerks now work at the same time, so the bank handles far more customers. The clever rule is that all of Rajesh's entries always go into the same book, so his personal history stays in perfect order even while the overall bank runs in parallel.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Partitions are the single idea that lets Kafka be both massively parallel and correctly ordered at the same time. A consumer group can have at most as many active consumers as there are partitions, so if a topic has twelve partitions, up to twelve consumers process it simultaneously, giving roughly twelve times the throughput of a single-partition topic. At National Bank of India, the transactions topic has twelve partitions, and four instances of the settlement service share them, each processing three partitions in parallel.

Scalability comes from distributing partitions across brokers. Each broker holds only a subset of the partitions, so both data and processing load scale with the cluster size. The third benefit is ordering control: Kafka guarantees strict ordering within a partition, and you control which records share a partition by choosing the message key. Keying by account id means Rajesh's debit always comes before his balance check, while Priya's events process independently on a different partition.

The senior insight is that choosing the partition count and the key is a real design decision. Too few partitions caps throughput and cannot be increased without breaking key ordering. Too many partitions add broker overhead. A good key like account id distributes load evenly across partitions while keeping per-entity ordering intact.

Remember one sentence: partitions give Kafka parallelism through multiple consumers, scalability through distributed brokers, and ordering through key-based routing, and choosing the partition count and key is one of the most important design decisions you make.
